item.title: France and Germany are lowering the banner of free trade themselves: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 23:38:00
The European Union (EU) flags in front of EU headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG By lowering the banner of free trade that they have upheld for more than half a century, France and Germany are betraying and negating their own principles. Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself. By wielding what it once condemned as a weapon, Europe is tarnishing its self-proclaimed image as "a defender of multilateralism." According to media reports, France and Germany submitted an informal paper to the European Commission on Monday, calling for stronger EU trade defense instruments. They seek to grant the Commission new powers to restrict or even revoke access to the EU single market for countries deemed to be engaging in "systemic market-distorting practices," as well as to establish mechanisms to "limit companies' reliance on single sources for certain critical supplies." Although the document does not name China, it is obvious to anyone with discernment who the target is. This joint push by France and Germany - the "twin engines" of the EU - is steering Europe down the wrong path of protectionism. By lowering the banner of free trade that they have upheld for more than half a century, France and Germany are betraying and negating their own principles. Europe is the birthplace of the modern concept of free trade and has been the most steadfast builder of the postwar multilateral trading system. From the customs union to the single market, from successive rounds of multilateral negotiations to the global circulation of the euro, openness has always been the bedrock of Europe's economic prosperity. In 2025, the EU trade in goods balance registered a surplus of 128 billion euros. As recently as June, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in the Bundestag that "Europe benefits more than any other continent in the world from open and fair global trade." His words are still ringing in our ears, yet four months later, he signed a joint paper claiming that the "existing trade toolbox is no longer sufficient." Using rules when they suit one's purposes and discarding them when they do not - treating rules as tools to be taken or left as needed - is tantamount to destroying one's own reputation. The EU is transforming from a victim of unilateralism into the very kind of perpetrator it once opposed. Back in 1998, the European Communities filed a complaint with the World Trade Organization regarding compliance with the US "Section 301" Trade Act, insisting that unilateral retaliatory measures must be subject to multilateral authorization. This case is still regarded today as a landmark precedent curbing unilateralism. Now, 28 years later, the former plaintiff is forging its own European version of "Section 301," using a "reverse qualified majority" mechanism to allow the European Commission's restrictive measures to take effect by default, which makes it difficult for member states to block them. One German official has unabashedly referred to it as a "second-strike weapon" to counter the escalation of the trade war. Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself. By wielding what it once condemned as a weapon, Europe is tarnishing its self-proclaimed image as "a defender of multilateralism." France and Germany's shift toward protectionism is, at its core, an attempt to package their own structural problems as "external threats." High energy prices, heavy regulatory costs and slow innovation upgrading are the real internal causes behind Europe's declining industrial competitiveness. A survey conducted in Germany shows that investment appetite among German small and medium-sized enterprises has already fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1995. Blaming others for the unfinished business of domestic reform and using trade barriers to compensate for lost cost advantages are less a "wake-up call" than an act of evasion. Germany's transformation from a "brake" on tough trade measures against China to today's "driving force" represents an attempt to treat internal ailments with external remedies - a failure to face its own problems head-on. The bill for protectionism will ultimately be paid by those who issue it. According to the latest survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China, about 33 percent of the companies surveyed believe their operations in China will be significantly affected if the EU-China trade negotiations fail to yield substantive results. French cognac sales have fallen from 230 million bottles since 2023 to 140 million bottles, a direct consequence of the countermeasures triggered by the EU's tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The experience of the US Section 301 tariffs offers an equally clear warning: Importers bore almost all of the costs, while the protected industries saw only marginal increases in output. Tariffs may be imposed on others, but the costs ultimately end up on one's own books. German companies, French distilleries and European consumers will all find their names on the bill. The ball remains in the EU's half of the court. The way forward lies at the negotiating table, not in a toolbox. China and Europe are deeply integrated through industrial and supply chains, making their economic and trade relationship fundamentally one of mutual benefit. Mutual dependence between China and the EU is not a risk, and intertwined interests are not a threat. Openness and cooperation are the right paths to development. European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic will visit China, and China-EU trade and investment consultations are still underway, demonstrating that the door to dialogue remains open. It is hoped that France and Germany, as major global economies, will uphold open cooperation and free trade, abide by WTO rules, refrain from urging the EU to reach for protectionist instruments at every turn, and avoid politicizing or securitizing economic and trade issues. Protectionism cannot boost competitiveness; decoupling and cutting off supply chains will only hurt others without benefiting oneself. Taking the wrong approach down the wrong path will ultimately backfire.

item.title: Tsai and Pelosi: A 'reunion' out of step with the times
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 23:13:00
Illustration: Liu Rui/GT Tsai Ing-wen. Nancy Pelosi. Former Taiwan regional leader. Former US House speaker. A pair of "old friends" recycling the same old script against the times. It has been reported that Tsai, the former leader of the Taiwan region, embarked on a week-long visit to the US on Monday local time. A politically "symbolic" stop on her itinerary occurred on Tuesday when she met with former US House speaker Pelosi. Tsai referred to Pelosi as an "old friend," while Pelosi declared that the "bond" between the US and the Taiwan region is "strong." For both, the meeting comes with their own political calculations. Tong Liqun, a research fellow at the Institute for Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao Studies of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Global Times that with Taiwan's local elections approaching in November, Tsai is attempting to invoke Pelosi's provocative 2022 visit, showcasing the so-called "achievements" of relying on the US to seek "Taiwan independence." She aims to revive public memories of her political legacy, and carve out space in the election narrative. For Pelosi, who has been marginalized in US politics, her previous visit to Taiwan was considered a defining episode of her political career. Thus, the meeting offers her another platform to reassert a political role from the past. However, the hollow political symbols of four years ago no longer align with the reality of today. During her provocative visit to Taiwan, Pelosi sought to send a signal that the US would not "abandon" Taiwan. Four years later, both women have faded from the centers of power, and their old script regarding the US and the Taiwan region has already been abandoned by the broader tide of history. What did the strategy of relying on external powers to seek "Taiwan independence" actually bring to peace across the Taiwan Straits? What Tsai seeks to evoke is less a glorious memory than a reminder of the heavy costs of that approach. The policies of "relying on the US to seek 'Taiwan independence'" and the "anti-China" stance pursued under both Tsai and the current Lai authorities are to blame for the instability in the Taiwan Straits in recent years. Pelosi's 2022 visit fostered an illusion on the island that the US would "protect" Taiwan. However, Beijing responded firmly to this politically speculative gamble with legitimate sanctions and military drills at that time, and the political leverage some in the DPP had hoped to gain from US support never materialized. The reality of 2022 had already exposed the limits of their calculations. Four years later, the Tsai-Pelosi reunion offers little reason to believe otherwise. The reunion runs counter to the realities facing both the Taiwan region and the US today. Zheng Jian, a professor at the Graduate Institute for Taiwan Studies at Xiamen University, said the approach of "relying on the US to seek 'Taiwan independence'" runs counter to the mainstream desire among Taiwan residents for peace and stability across the Taiwan Straits, the US core interest in avoiding confrontation with China and safeguarding its own interests, as well as the broader trend toward China's national reunification. Following the China-US summit in September, the two heads of state agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, sending a clear signal that Beijing and Washington are seeking to put guardrails around competition and preserve channels of communication amid differences. Zheng added that against this backdrop, more residents in Taiwan are beginning to reconsider the risks brought by the path of "relying on the US to seek 'independence'": Is it wiser to remain on the front line of conflict risks, or return to the path of peaceful cross-Straits development? A recent Taiwan poll found that 60 percent of respondents on the island had no confidence in the US "protecting" Taiwan's interests, while only about one-quarter expressed confidence. The findings underscore the declining credibility of the narrative long promoted by the DPP authorities. Four years ago, Pelosi's Taiwan visit was a political show staged by an aging Western political figure for personal gains. Today, Tsai and Pelosi, the two aging "former" leaders remain immersed in the old script, attempting to revive their political legacies and influence. Their meeting is little more than a politically convenient performance - two faded political figures cling to a spotlight that has already moved on.

item.title: Tokyo reportedly mulls nuclear subs amid security document revision; 'could spur arms race'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 23:06:00
Demonstrators stage a rally before the Diet against the Japanese government's nuclear policies in Tokyo, Japan, on November 21, 2025. Protesters also call on the government to join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Photo: VCG As Japan prepares to revise its three security documents by year-end, including the National Security Strategy, plans have emerged within the Japanese government to mention nuclear submarines as an option for strengthening deterrence, Kyodo News reported on Tuesday, citing several sources familiar with the matter. The Japanese government may avoid directly mentioning Japan's "possession" of nuclear submarines, instead limiting the language to "further research and discussions" according to Kyodo News. Yomiuri Shimbun reported on Wednesday that the plan is expected to take several years before a final decision is made on whether to formally acquire the equipment. Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, said that if Japan were to introduce nuclear submarines, its military capabilities would undergo a significant shift toward a more offensive posture. Since nuclear submarines offer extended submerged endurance, high-speed mobility and long-range operational capabilities, they could serve as highly concealed platforms for precision standoff strikes against land and maritime targets if they are equipped with vertical launch systems and long-range or hypersonic weapons, Zhang said. The combination of these capabilities could shift Japan's self-claimed exclusively defense-oriented policy toward greater strategic deterrence and long-range strike capabilities, potentially altering the military balance in East Asia. Such a shift could spur neighboring countries to boost defense spending and expand anti-submarine and long-range strike capabilities, fueling an arms race and heightening regional security tensions, Zhang added. Successive Japanese governments have limited the use of nuclear energy to peaceful purposes under the country's Atomic Energy Basic Act, prohibiting nuclear to be used for military purposes. Given the expected massive spending, strong caution remains within the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), per Kyodo News. Da Zhigang, a research fellow at the Institute of Northeast Asian Studies of the Heilongjiang Academy of Social Sciences, pointed out that an explicit reference in its security documents to studying nuclear submarines could signal that the Takaichi administration is testing public opinion and laying the policy groundwork for eventually acquiring US-built or domestically developed nuclear subs. Knowing that Japanese society, as well as its neighboring countries, remains wary of any attempt by Japan to revise its Three Non-Nuclear Principles or seek to acquire nuclear weapons, Takaichi administration is testing the waters step by step, Da told the Global Times on Wednesday. Such tentative actions to strengthen its nuclear capabilities could raise tension and spur further military buildup in the region, Da added. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said in September that Japan would "not rule out any options" in discussions and studies on whether to acquire nuclear-powered submarines as part of a revision of the country's key security documents, Xinhua reported, citing Kyodo News. In response to that, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a press briefing on September 30 that the "no-nuclear-taboo" remark is a blatant provocation and serious stomp on the Non-Proliferation Treaty and the postwar international order. It is diametrically opposed to the three non-nuclear principles that Japan claims to uphold. His remark once again revealed the Japanese right-wing pursuit of a nuclear Japan. The international community needs to call on Japan to strictly observe the three non-nuclear principles, fulfill its obligations under the NPT, abandon remilitarization and its nuclear ambitions, and earnestly respond to the concerns of the international community, Guo said.

item.title: Major three-part documentary chronicles China's efforts on combating Myanmar telecom fraud, promoting global co-op
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 22:53:00
Photo: Xinhua From the downfall of the notorious "four major families" criminal gangs in northern Myanmar to joint operations targeting fraud compounds in Myanmar's Myawaddy and the establishment of an international anti-fraud mechanism initiated by China, a major three-part documentary airing on the Chinese state broadcaster offers a rare, in-depth look at how China's years-long fight against cross-border telecom fraud has evolved from dismantling major criminal strongholds to promoting broader international law-enforcement cooperation. Jointly produced by China's Ministry of Public Security (MPS) and China Media Group, the documentary chronicles the arduous process and major achievements of Chinese public security authorities and relevant departments in combating criminal groups targeting Chinese citizens from bases in northern Myanmar, including through cooperation with law-enforcement authorities of relevant countries, according to the official WeChat account of the Criminal Investigation Bureau of the MPS. Across three episodes, the documentary follows a clear trajectory: exposing the brutal criminal ecosystem behind telecom fraud compounds in northern Myanmar, pursuing and bringing major criminal groups to justice across borders, and expanding international cooperation aimed at preventing such crimes from taking root again. The first episode exposes the dark reality behind the once-rampant fraud compounds. People lured or trafficked into the compounds were chillingly referred to as "piglets." Some were subjected to electric shocks, violence and tight control. In one particularly disturbing scene, a member of a criminal group brazenly compares fraudsters and their victims to predators and prey, saying that wolves are born to eat meat, while lions are meant to eat sheep. The details reveal how telecom fraud in northern Myanmar had developed far beyond individual online scams into an organized criminal ecosystem involving fraud compounds, armed control and multiple forms of serious crime. The second episode shifts the focus from what happened inside the compounds to how Chinese authorities pursued criminals entrenched overseas. It documents how Chinese judicial and law-enforcement authorities worked to overcome geographical and law-enforcement barriers and, through cooperation with other countries, bring suspects back to face justice. Since 2023, China and Myanmar have carried out joint operations that led to the dismantling of four major criminal gangs in Myanmar's Kokang region, according to the Criminal Investigation Bureau of the MPS. From October last year to August this year, the number of telecom fraud cases in China declined year-on-year for 11 consecutive months. By the end of 2025, Chinese courts had concluded first-instance trials of more than 27,000 cases related to telecom fraud operations in northern Myanmar, with more than 41,000 repatriated suspects sentenced, according to China's Supreme People's Court, the Xinhua News Agency reported. The Ming and Bai groups have completed all judicial proceedings, with 39 individuals receiving sentences of life imprisonment or heavier penalties, including 16 sentenced to death. The two cross-border armed criminal rings were completely dismantled, the Supreme People's Court said in February. Expanded collaboration However, the downfall of the major criminal groups in northern Myanmar did not mark the end of China's anti-fraud campaign. As intensified law-enforcement operations squeezed established fraud hubs, preventing criminal networks from rebuilding their operations elsewhere became an increasingly pressing challenge. China's response has therefore expanded from domestic investigations and bilateral law-enforcement cooperation toward deeper regional and international coordination. The third and final episode turns the focus to a broader challenge - how to prevent cross-border fraud networks from relocating, regrouping and returning after major criminal strongholds have been dismantled. One striking case unfolded in Muse in northern Myanmar, just across the border from Southwest China's Yunnan Province. The documentary shows that a high-rise building housing telecom fraud operations stood less than 200 meters from the Jiegao border port in Ruili. By around the Spring Festival of 2024, Chinese police had obtained clear indications that the building had been occupied by fraud groups that had resumed operations under new guises. But the problem went beyond individual compounds. The documentary shows how cross-border fraud groups displayed a strong ability to regenerate even after successive crackdowns. In July 2024, an accountant at a company in Zhuji, East China's Zhejiang Province, was tricked into transferring 17 million yuan ($2.4 million) after an overseas fraud group planted malware on her computer, remotely monitored it and impersonated her company chairman. Police investigations traced the operation to a fraud compound in the so-called "Fourth Special Region" in northern Myanmar, where fraud operations had resurfaced following an earlier crackdown. Using the case as the lead, Chinese and Myanmar law-enforcement authorities swiftly launched a joint operation, dismantling compounds linked to dozens of similar cases nationwide and capturing a number of key figures behind the overseas operations. Yunnan police subsequently signed a border law-enforcement cooperation agreement with relevant authorities in Myanmar's border region, helping establish a regular joint crackdown mechanism aimed at dynamically clearing fraud compounds targeting China. "We are not afraid of them resurfacing. If they emerge, we will strike," Zhang Jun, then head of the telecom and online fraud investigation division under the Criminal Investigation Bureau of the MPS, said in the documentary. Such cooperation has continued to expand. Since 2023, Chinese and Myanmar police have continued to deepen law-enforcement cooperation, with more than 59,000 Chinese nationals suspected of fraud arrested and handed over to China, while the notorious "four major families" criminal gangs in Kokang region were completely dismantled. In early 2025, China, Myanmar and Thailand established a ministerial-level coordination mechanism for jointly combating telecom fraud and subsequently carried out 10 joint repatriation operations. More recently, with the active efforts of China's MPS, law-enforcement authorities from the three countries carried out their first joint cleanup operation targeting telecom fraud compounds in Myanmar's Myawaddy. More than 630 buildings in the notorious KK Park have since been completely demolished, according to Xinhua. The progression documented in the final episode - from China-Myanmar joint operations and a regular border law-enforcement mechanism to coordinated operations involving China, Myanmar and Thailand - shows how the response has evolved alongside the increasingly transnational nature of telecom fraud. Such cooperation is now expanding beyond individual operations and neighboring countries toward a broader multilateral mechanism. On September 10, the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud, initiated by the Chinese government, was established in Lianyungang, East China's Jiangsu Province. Representatives from 46 founding countries, 34 observer countries and four international organizations, including the United Nations and Interpol, attended its inaugural conference. The alliance is an intergovernmental organization designed to promote cooperation among law-enforcement agencies in tackling transnational telecom and cyber fraud and related crimes, Xinhua reported. The expansion of international cooperation is crucial as fraud syndicates seek new footholds under mounting law-enforcement pressure. Some criminal groups squeezed out of parts of Southeast Asia have increasingly relocated to regions including the Middle East, Africa and Central America, according to the MPS. The cooperation China has helped advance is also moving beyond neighboring countries and individual operations toward a broader multilateral framework. This year alone, China carried out its first such joint law-enforcement operations with US and UAE police, dismantling nine fraud compounds and arresting 276 suspects. China has also worked with Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia and Sri Lanka, among other countries, with more than 20,000 telecom and online fraud suspects arrested and repatriated. Taken together, the three episodes document an evolution in China's fight against telecom fraud - from dismantling major criminal groups and overseas compounds to cutting cross-border criminal chains and building mechanisms for sustained international law-enforcement cooperation. This year marks the beginning of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), with combating and governing telecom and online fraud listed among the priorities for public security work during the period. The establishment of the 46-country alliance, together with expanding bilateral and trilateral law-enforcement cooperation, points to sustained international coordination as an increasingly important part of that effort.

item.title: China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation on infectious diseases prevention: Chinese FM on plague case in Siberia
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 22:42:00
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation on the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including plague, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Tuesday in response to a question concerning a plague infection incident in Russia. An employee of a Russian anti-plague institute in the remote Siberian region of Irkutsk has reportedly died of a suspected pneumonic plague infection. The US State Department said that they are monitoring the situation closely. Guo made the remarks when asked whether Russian authorities are reaching out to Chinese authorities and experts on possible cooperation to deal with this problem. Global Times

item.title: GT Voice: South Korea's space endeavors draw rising attention from Asia
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 22:35:00
A view of Seoul, South Korea's capital city, in Autumn Photo: VCG South Korea launched its homegrown Nuri rocket for a fifth time on Wednesday, sending a record of 15 satellites into orbit, the Yonhap News Agency reported. The launch was Nuri's first attempt to deploy multiple primary satellites in space. The role of private companies such as Hanwha Aerospace significantly expanded in this latest launch, marking another critical step in transitioning the government-developed Nuri into a space transportation system led by the country's private enterprises. The country's intention to rely more heavily on the private sector to advance its space ambitions has drawn international attention to its ongoing industrial transformation. For a long time, South Korea's space efforts were led by state-owned research institutions, with core technology development and launch missions coordinated through official channels. But this time, Hanwha Aerospace, the rocket's prime systems contractor, expanded its role beyond manufacturing and final assembly to actual launch operations, according to South Korean media reports. It was a significant step toward a space industrial system led by the private sector, a deliberate push to build up a commercial space sector and a complete space supply chain. It's worth watching how far and how fast that transition will proceed. The first reason the transition is worth anticipating lies in the market. The global commercial space sector is witnessing explosive growth in low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite constellations, Earth observation and space research missions. The Asia-Pacific region stands out as the world's fastest-growing commercial space market. According to Global View Research, the global LEO satellite market is projected to reach $41.31 billion by 2033, with a compound annual growth rate of 14 percent from 2025 to 2033. The LEO satellite market in the Asia-Pacific region is expected to register the fastest annual growth rate of more than 17 percent from 2025 to 2033. Rapid digital transformation and regional cooperation in space are key drivers behind this region's expanding LEO satellite footprint. South Korea's commercial space sector evolution will draw rising attention from other parts of the world. Benefiting from its relatively comprehensive industrial system, its sophisticated electronics sector in particular, the country boasts solid cost-control capabilities in satellite manufacturing and ground equipment development. As a latecomer to space explorations, South Korea may prove more flexible in adopting new technologies and modern business models. That combination could be precisely the foundation for differentiated competition in space. Nevertheless, the leap from successful rocket launches to viable commercial service contracts involves far more than technological reliability. It also requires accumulated market credibility, resilient industrial supply chain and highly efficient and standardized operational systems - all important thresholds for South Korea's space industry to cross. Even so, the strategic value of South Korea's commercial space launches lies in pushing the international space market further toward diversification. A diversified market ecosystem can drive faster technological iteration, service upgrading and price optimization, offering global customers more launch options and service solutions. The external environment in Asia is also favorable. Asia's expanding commercial space activities are creating greater opportunities for the regional division of labor and fostering collaborative chances, with different economies excelling in rocket manufacturing, satellite development and space data applications. If South Korea can integrate into this regional ecosystem, its commercial space development will become part of Asia's overall competitiveness. Ultimately, commercial space is a field where trust accumulates over the long term. If South Korea can move beyond technology validation toward institutionalized transparency and broader cooperation — say releasing more concrete, businesslike information about its future missions — it will not only shore up its own commercial space ecosystem construction but also inject new momentum into the positive interaction of Asia's regional industrial chain.

item.title: Documentary discloses the moments when hoods removed after ringleader and key members of major cross-border gambling and fraud criminal syndicate escorted back to China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 22:32:00
Chen Zhi Photo: Screenshot from CCTV The moments when Chen Zhi, the ringleader of a major cross-border gambling and fraud criminal syndicate based in Cambodia and two other key members of the group were escorted back to China and had their hoods removed was disclosed in the third episode of a major documentary aired by China’s state broadcaster. The series, titled “The Demise of Myanmar-Based Telecom Fraud,” was aired from Monday to Wednesday by China Central Television (CCTV). The CCTV video shows that on January 7, 2026, China’s Ministry of Public Security dispatched a working group to escort Chen, founder of Cambodian business empire the Prince Group, from Phnom Penh back to China. On April 1, Li Xiong, a key member of the criminal syndicate, was repatriated from Phnom Penh to China, followed by Liu Ren, another key member of the criminal group, on June 17. Chinese police have vowed to maintain a relentless crackdown on telecom fraud and called on governments worldwide to work together to combat the crime, CCTV reported. The Prince Group, operated by Chen, claims itself as a multinational business conglomerate with investments in resorts, hotels and other projects in Cambodia. It is one of the country’s largest corporate groups. However, the group actually lured workers with fake job advertisements, tortured them and forced them to conduct telecom scams, in which victims were tricked into transferring cryptocurrency in exchange for huge investment returns they are promised, Beijing Daily reported. In 2016, Chen directed Liu and others to establish the Jin Bei Group in Cambodia. The group operated multiple online gambling platforms, aggressively soliciting Chinese citizens to participate in online gambling. Since 2020, Jin Bei Group has operated scam compounds in Cambodia and carried out large-scale telecom and online fraud involving vast sums of money. In addition, Liu is also suspected of serious violent crimes, including unlawful detention and intentional assault, Beijing Daily reported. Li, former chairman of Huione Group, a subsidiary of Prince Group, is suspected of multiple crimes, including operating casinos, fraud, illegal business operations, and concealing or disguising the criminal proceeds, per Beijing Daily. The documentary is jointly produced by China’s Ministry of Public Security and China Media Group. The three-episode documentary series offers an unprecedented look into the horrific reality of Myanmar cyber fraud networks, as well as China’s determination and relentless crackdown on notorious cross-border cyber-scam operations. Global Times

item.title: Two pandas arrive in Atlanta, carrying decades of shared care and friendship that keep crossing borders
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 22:30:00
Giant panda Fu Shuang was doing little more than sitting and eating bamboo. When she seemed to notice the camera, she paused, cast a sideways glance toward it, then picked up another bamboo stalk and went back to eating. Zoo Atlanta posted the less-than-50-second clip on TikTok days after Fu Shuang arrived from China with male panda Ping Ping. Within days, the video had received more than 120,000 likes and around 1,500 comments. "I cannot express how excited I am about having pandas at the zoo again! I cannot wait to see them!" one TikTok user wrote. The wait now has a date. On Tuesday local time, Zoo Atlanta announced that Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will make their public debut on November 6 at the newly renovated Arthur M. Blank Panda Grove. The pair are currently completing routine quarantine and acclimatization. Ping Ping and Fu Shuang arrived in Atlanta on September 27 after flying from Chengdu, Southwest China's Sichuan Province. Their journey drew wide attention from both Chinese and US media. Their arrival marks the return of giant pandas to Atlanta nearly two years after the zoo's previous panda family returned to China, according to ABC News. A chartered flight carrying giant pandas Fu Shuang and Ping Ping arrives in Atlanta, the US, on September 27, 2026. Photo: Zoo Atlanta The new arrivals also continue a much longer story. Zoo Atlanta's previous cooperation with China began in 1999 and lasted 25 years, during which giant pandas Lun Lun and Yang Yang raised seven cubs, the Global Times learned from the National Forestry and Grassland Administration. The history stretches back even further. In 1972, Ling Ling and Hsing Hsing arrived in the US following then US president Richard Nixon's visit to China, beginning one of the most recognizable chapters in people-to-people exchanges between the two countries, according to the Xinhua News Agency. Over the decades, giant panda cooperation has grown beyond public fascination with the animals. China has carried out giant panda conservation and research cooperation with zoos around the world, covering breeding, disease prevention, scientific research, personnel training, and the protection of wild populations and habitats. Yet the pandas themselves remain at the center of that connection. From crowds waiting outside overseas zoos to fans traveling to Sichuan to see pandas after they return to China, the black-and-white bears have continued to draw people across borders - sometimes long after the journey of a particular panda has ended. Starting a new life Ping Ping and Fu Shuang did not simply board a plane and begin a new life in the US. The two six-year-old giant pandas had already spent weeks preparing for the journey before leaving Chengdu, according to the National Forestry and Grassland Administration. Ping Ping, a male born on March 17, 2020, is recognizable by his broad, dark eye patches. Though stout, he is agile and especially fond of climbing trees and resting among the branches. Fu Shuang, born on October 18 the same year, has a small tuft of fluffy hair on her head and is quick at locating food hidden by keepers as part of enrichment activities. Both were born at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. Ahead of departure, the pair underwent around a month of quarantine and preparation at the Chengdu base. Keepers monitored their condition and trained them to become familiar with noises they might encounter in transit. They also practiced entering their travel crates on command. The Chengdu base indicated that such training was intended to reduce stress and avoid difficulties on departure day, CCTV reported. When the dedicated FedEx "Panda Express" Boeing 777 left Chengdu on September 27, fresh bamboo, bamboo shoots, apples and emergency medicines were among the supplies prepared for the trip. Their new home had been prepared with similar attention. Chinese and US specialists held repeated discussions over the enclosure and its facilities before the pandas arrived. Zoo Atlanta has since confirmed that the renovation of what is now called the Arthur M. Blank Panda Grove cost $6 million. Indoor dayrooms were expanded and upgraded with new climbing structures and pools, while the outdoor habitats also received new climbing features and landscaping. The new complex is scheduled to open to visitors on November 6. For now, much of the work is taking place out of public view. Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are completing routine quarantine while adapting to unfamiliar sounds, smells, spaces and keepers. Chinese personnel will remain at the zoo for three months to assist with quarantine, stress adaptation and behavioral training, according to the National Forestry and Grassland Administration. A giant panda enjoys bamboo at Zoo Atlanta in the US in February 2024. Photo: VCG That process is part of a broader system of cooperation. Li Desheng, deputy director of the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda, told the Global Times in an earlier interview that overseas partners regularly report on pandas' health and consult Chinese specialists when conditions change. Keepers, he said, pay close attention to how individual animals respond to food, people and new surroundings, then adjust care accordingly. In Atlanta, that long-standing practice is now being applied to the latest pair beginning their decade-long stay. Li said that kind of care ultimately depends on trust. He described the goal as treating them almost like family or friends, building trust into everyday health management. For Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, that patient process is now beginning again with a new group of keepers in Atlanta. Nurtured through partnership Ten years ago, on September 3, 2016, keepers at Zoo Atlanta watched Lun Lun give birth at 7:20 am. Then, 47 minutes later, a second cub arrived. Panda newborns are tiny and vulnerable, and raising twins presents a particular challenge: A mother in the wild will generally care for only one. At the zoo, one cub stayed with Lun Lun while the other received care in a nursery; the team then exchanged them so both could spend time with their mother, the Zoo Atlanta documented. Two colleagues from the Chengdu breeding base joined the nursery team. The cubs became Lun Lun and Yang Yang's sixth and seventh offspring. That shared work reaches beyond one enclosure. Li remembers being at the San Diego Zoo when Hua Mei was born on August 21, 1999. He recalled the excitement among the staff and the chance to learn from American colleagues whose experience with other wildlife brought different ideas to the panda program. Hua Mei, conceived through artificial insemination, became the first US-born panda cub to survive to adulthood. She later returned to China and had 11 cubs of her own, according to a review by the San Diego Zoo's wildlife team. For Li, the excitement of her birth remains one of the moments he recalls most clearly from years of working with overseas colleagues. A giant panda enjoys bamboo at Zoo Atlanta in the US in February 2024. Photo: VCG The collaboration has also been tested when an animal needed treatment. In 2014, veterinarians at the San Diego Zoo operated on Gao Gao after finding a cancerous tumor in one of his testicles. The case involved the care of an individual panda, while the longer partnership allowed Chinese and American teams to exchange veterinary and husbandry experience. Li told the Global Times that scientists on both sides had learned from one another through such work, as well as through breeding and disease-prevention research. A birth during the pandemic showed another way teams can work together across distance. South Korea had not previously managed a panda birth when Fu Bao was born at Everland in 2020. Chinese specialists provided guidance remotely, while Wu Kai, a keeper from the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda, worked on site with local staff. Fu Bao developed a rash when she was about 10 days old, and her eyes opened earlier than expected. The teams continued caring for her through those early concerns, according to Li. Years later, her return to China would bring many of the people who had followed her throughout her childhood in South Korea to Sichuan. At Zoo Atlanta, the earlier partnership encompassed more than 30 joint research projects and over 50 papers, according to China's National Forestry and Grassland Administration. Work covered cub rearing, behavior research and disease prevention, alongside efforts related to wild pandas and their habitats. The figures sit behind recognizable moments: a second twin arriving 47 minutes after the first, a keeper exchanging cubs between nursery and mother panda, and colleagues staying close as a panda adjusts to a new home. Ping Ping and Fu Shuang's arrival begins another period in which those routines will be carried out together. Following pandas home For some American panda lovers, a panda's return to China has become the reason for a journey of their own. Tai Shan, born at the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington in 2005, drew crowds when he left for China in 2010. According to China Green Times, some of his followers have continued traveling to Sichuan for his birthdays. A panda they first met at a zoo in the US remains part of their calendar years after his departure. South Korean vlogger Kim Soo-kyung made her way to Sichuan when Fu Bao appeared before visitors after returning from South Korea. Kim told the Global Times that she could hear her own heartbeat when she saw the panda again. She began filming Fu Bao for followers who could not make the trip. Followers who could not make the trip asked in the comments how the panda was doing. At the base, Kim also met fans from different places. They made postcards and birthday decorations, while a Chinese fan who saw one of her posts sent her Fu Bao souvenirs. Her videos kept a conversation going between people who had watched the same panda from different countries. Xiang Xiang's Japanese admirers are still following her across the sea. On June 12, the Japan-born giant panda celebrated her ninth birthday at the Ya'an Bifengxia base in Sichuan. Around 200 panda fans visited the base that morning, including Japanese fans who had traveled to China to mark the occasion. Their wishes were simple: "Happy birthday" and "May you always be well." Giant panda Xiang Xiang meets fans in Ya'an, Sichuan Province. Photo: VCG The celebration was happening in Japan, too. In Tokyo, nearly 300 people, including Ueno Zoo representatives, panda conservationists, photographers and fans, gathered for a Xiang Xiang family birthday event, the China News Service reported. An affection that began with a visit to a panda base led Suzanne Braden, an American conservation supporter, much further. Li recalled that, while he was working with colleagues at the San Diego Zoo, Braden sought him out to learn about the Chinese people caring for pandas. They spent hours talking. Braden later co-founded Pandas International. After the 2008 Wenchuan quake damaged the Wolong Panda Center, her organization was among the first to provide aid, according to Michigan State University. Li said Braden's response after the earthquake was something that had stayed with him for years. "The friendship formed through giant pandas and the help they gave us are deeply etched in our hearts," Li said. "Even after so many years, it remains unforgettable."

item.title: China's railways record more than 250 mln passenger trips during Mid-Autumn Festival, National Day holidays
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 20:50:00
Beijing braces for National Day holidays return travel peak, well-prepared extended transit services ready Photo: Li Hao/Global Times "Tourist marvels, local cuisine, educational activities for the kids, and a bit of tech... these are the key words for my family's trip to Datong," said 30-something Pan Li, a Beijing resident who just wrapped up a family self-driving tour to the culturally rich city in North China's Shanxi Province. Pan's story is not alone. From family trips and scenic viewing to rural retreats and unique cultural experiences, hundreds of millions of Chinese people hit the road during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays breaks. The three-day Mid-Autumn Festival holidays ran from September 25 to September 27, and the week-long National Day holidays ran from October 1 to 7. For those who took a three-day annual leave, the holiday could be lengthened to a total of 13 days. Industry insiders and analysts said this year's "Golden Week" holidays clearly showed the holiday economy's impact on revitalizing the real economy and optimizing consumption patterns, boosting China's ongoing recovery. With a great many Chinese tourists going abroad, major global destinations also saw a marked rise in Chinese visitors, prompting many businesses to roll out catered services. Domestic travel binge Tourists enjoy themselves as Longli Prairie in Qiannan Bouyei and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, Southwest China's Guizhou Province, is bathed in a sky full of red clouds, on the morning of October 7, 2026. Photo: VCG The holiday economy's bustle is reflected in numbers, from transport to box office to sports tournament ticket sales. China's railways recorded more than 250 million passenger trips from September 23 to Tuesday, as the holiday period wrapped up, China State Railway Group Co said on Wednesday. Wednesday marked the final day of China's National Day holidays, with the railway operator expecting to handle 24.15 million passenger trips. According to online platform data, total box office revenue for the 2026 National Day holiday period surpassed 1.1 billion yuan ($164 million), CCTV News reported on Wednesday. This year's holidays were characterized by more Chinese people making longer trips in search of richer experiences. Nearly 30 percent of travelers booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged over 50 percent year-on-year, according to a statement sent to the Global Times on Wednesday by online travel platform Qunar. Demand for long-distance travel has soared, while cultural and tourism consumption vouchers across regions continued to stimulate spending, according to a report provided by domestic platform Tongcheng Travel to the Global Times on Wednesday. Overnight stays, autumn sightseeing, and county-level tourism all flourished, alongside a simultaneous rise in outbound and inbound travel. Shanghai LEGOLAND Resort said that due to the longer holidays, it maintained high overall visitor numbers, with daily attendance records repeatedly refreshed and October 5 setting an all-time high for single-day visitors. There was a year-on-year increase in visitors from distant regions and overseas, with its LEGOLAND Hotel fully booked for five consecutive days, the park said in a statement sent to the Global Times on Wednesday. Wang Peng, an associate research fellow at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Wednesday that this year's National Day holiday consumption market showed thriving supply and demand and coordinated growth across multiple sectors. From cultural and tourism experiences and brick-and-mortar commercial districts to big-ticket consumption, all areas gained momentum. "It is not pulse-like growth in a single sector, but a concentrated reflection of the continuous optimization of the consumption structure and steadily strengthening endogenous market momentum, laying a micro-level foundation for the economy's full-year recovery and improvement," Wang said. "The advantages of China's super-large market continued to be unleashed, services consumption became the core growth engine, policy support effects were precisely delivered, and supply-side innovation continued to invigorate vitality," the expert added. Changing pattern Paying for experience and an increasing level of technology have become standout features of travel during this year's National Day holidays, tourists and industry experts told the Global Times. Pan, the Beijing tourist, said her family of three spent some 8,000 yuan on a seven-day trip. Much of the expense went to experiences: medicinal cuisine, virtual reality cultural tours, and a hired guide. "The hired tour guide service is amazing, at around 500 yuan per tour. My daughter seems to have endless questions for our hired guide about the cultural relics we visited." By contrast, rigid expenses such as gasoline, tolls, and tourist site admission tickets went down, Pan said. Li Gang, a project lead with the Mount Tai scenic area, told the Global Times on Wednesday that some 2,000 tourists had tried his company's exoskeleton robots to climb the famous, steep mountain in East China's Shandong Province. At a price of 80 yuan, the high-tech gear greatly reduced fatigue for its wearers. Holidaymakers also showed profound interest in China's many counties endowed with tourist resources and unique culture. According to Qunar, during the combined holiday period, hotel bookings in Chinese counties rose by 35 percent year-on-year, with platform users staying at hotels in over a thousand counties nationwide. Top choices included Jiuzhaigou in Southwest China's Sichuan Province, Yangshuo in South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, and Burqin in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Hotel bookings in popular county seats across Xinjiang, Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, the Qinghai-Gansu region, and western Sichuan saw growth exceeding 50 percent. During the holidays, cultural and tourism consumption voucher campaigns further fueled the travel market. According to Tongcheng Travel, vouchers integrated on the platform from over 10 domestic destinations including those in South China's Guangdong Province and East China's Suzhou city exceeded 60 million yuan, marking a year-on-year increase of 325 percent. Inbound, outbound travel With a longer holiday, many Chinese embarked on overseas trips, and many foreign destinations braced for a wave of Chinese tourists. From Melbourne's Twelve Apostles beach to the Dolomites in Italy, Chinese tourists appeared in large crowds. Many netizens shared on Chinese social media that Chinese tourists could be seen everywhere at popular scenic spots worldwide, and that they could understand conversations around them, surrounded by their fellow countrymen. "The whole world knows that Chinese people are on holiday" became a trending topic on China's Sina Weibo social media platform. One Chinese tourist even said a tour to Iceland's Arctic wilderness contained only one foreigner - the tour guide, Beijing Business Today reported. According to Tongcheng Travel, Southeast Asian countries offering visa-free entry - such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand - along with South Korea, remained top choices for Chinese residents' outbound travel during the long holiday. Interest in North America, Europe, and the Australia and New Zealand region rose markedly. Multi-country tours saw booking volume surge over 60 percent year-on-year, with the average itinerary covering 2.8 countries and typically lasting more than seven days. South Korea's Asia Business Daily reported that accommodation booking platform AllMyTour analyzed reservations for the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays in mid-September and found that Chinese hotel bookings in Busan increased by 119.5 percent year-on-year. Tourism authorities in Thailand said they expected some 250,000 Chinese tourists will visit the country between September 25 and October 7, bringing in about 11.5 billion baht in tourism revenue. On the inbound side, more international travelers flocked to China to experience the country, riding a rising wave of global fascination with its scenery, culture, lifestyles, and, more recently, Chinese brands and design, according to the Xinhua News Agency. "From popular neighboring countries to long-haul overseas markets, Chinese tourists set foot in numerous destinations worldwide, and even many niche destinations were boosted in popularity… This has directly driven up revenue growth across local hotels, aviation, retail and the entire industrial chain," Wang said, noting that the long holiday facilitated two-way travel between Chinese and foreign tourists. Zhang Yiwu, a professor with Peking University, told the Global Times on Wednesday that the trend of prioritizing in-depth experiences is also notably evident in inbound tourism, with overseas visitors increasingly willing to venture into lesser-known regions to experience authentic China. "Along with an expanding range of immersive products and supplies, inbound tourism is emerging as a major new growth area," the professor said.

item.title: Indonesia reportedly expects Chinese J-10 fighter jets within six months; air force chief of staff urges public patience
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 17:10:00
Two J-10 fighter jets attached to an aviation brigade with the air force under the Chinese PLA Southern Theater Command taxi on the runway after returning from a nighttime flight training exercise in recent days. (eng.chinamil.com.cn/Photo by Xiao Rui) Indonesia's Air Force Chief of Staff reportedly told the public recently to be patient about the delivery of J-10 fighter jets from China, with an Indonesian media report saying the Chinese-made warplanes are expected to arrive in Indonesia within six months. An expert said the J-10CE fighter jet has attracted interest from several countries since its reported combat performance in May last year, thanks to its combat-proven capabilities and high cost-effectiveness. Indonesian Air Force Chief of Staff (KSAU) Air Marshal Mohamad Tonny Harjono asked the public to be patient regarding the arrival of Chengdu J-10 fighter jets from China, Indonesian media outlet Republika reported on Tuesday. "Just wait," Tonny was quoted by Republika as saying at the TNI Headquarters, Cilangkap, East Jakarta on Monday. Republika, citing its own information, reported that the fighter jets nicknamed the Vigorous Dragon are expected to arrive in Indonesia six months from now. However, the number of units arriving in Indonesia for the first time next year is still unknown. At the same location, a member of Commission I of the Indonesian House of Representatives supported the Indonesian Ministry of Defense's move to purchase J-10 fighter jets. He considered that purchasing 4.5-generation fighter jets from China could strengthen the defense of the country, according to the Republika report. In October 2025, Indonesia's Minister of Defense Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin confirmed that Indonesia is set to acquire Chengdu J-10 fighter jets from China, Indonesian news agency Antara reported at the time. In response to a related question, Zhang Xiaogang, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, said at a regular press conference in October 2025 that China has always taken a prudent and responsible attitude toward the export of military equipment. "We are willing to share the new achievements of our equipment development with peace-loving countries and jointly safeguard international and regional peace and stability," the spokesperson said. Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times that the J-10CE has drawn significant international attention after it has reportedly demonstrated its capabilities in the air combat between Pakistan and India in May 2025. One of the highlights of the J-10CE is its beyond-visual-range air combat capabilities when paired with the PL-15 series of air-to-air missiles. With the aircraft's outstanding radar detection capability, the PL-15 missile's range could be fully utilized, giving it an advantage in securing air superiority, Zhang said. The expert also noted that the J-10CE offers high cost-effectiveness, being more affordable than Western fighters of comparable capability. In August, Uzbek state media unveiled Chinese J-10CE fighters during the country's national celebration. O'zbekiston 24, a channel under Uzbekistan's state television and radio company, broadcast the event live. The released footage showed six J-10CE fighters being welcomed with a traditional water salute after landing. The aircraft bore the markings of the Uzbek military, Newshub.uz reported. Uzbekistan thus became the second confirmed overseas customer of the J-10CE, after Pakistan. Observers called this a breakthrough for advanced Chinese fighter jets in the international market, particularly in Central Asia. At the sixth Azerbaijan International Defense Exhibition, which opened at the Baku Expo Center on September 30 local time, the J-10CE fighter jet was among a range of Chinese-made aircraft being showcased. According to a photo released by Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), a model of a J-10CE was displayed with the national flag of Azerbaijan, with Zhang telling Global Times in a previous interview that it could suggest growing recognition of the fighter jet on the Azerbaijani side and raise the possibility that the two sides could eventually reach a procurement agreement. Bangladesh is also reportedly advancing plans to purchase Chinese-made J-10CE fighter jets. Bloomberg reported in August that a government negotiating committee had finalized a draft contract for the procurement of the multi-role combat aircraft. Bangladeshi media outlet Daily Sabah also reported that draft agreements covering the J-10CE and attack helicopters had been prepared and submitted to relevant authorities for approval.
